description: We are students from Griffith College Dublin, passionate about technology and innovations
summary: RedMark is a layered walk map for astronauts on Mars that also tells them where they are, with no GPS. It answers the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge for a two-person walk into the Gale crater boxwork on Mount Sharp. Five map layers built from NASA data (terrain and slope, walkability , science targets, conditions on the day , and our own location-quality layer) feed a planner that finds the f astest route that breaks no safety limit. On the way , the crew takes a photo and RedMark matches the skyline against 3D terrain to give a position with an honest uncertainty circle. Mars has no GPS, no compass and a radio delay of up to 24 minutes, so a crew that cannot fix its own position offline cannot walk f ar from the habitat safely . RedMark runs offline and shows where its position is reliable and where it is not.
details:
What it does

Mars has no GPS satellites. That's a real problem for astronauts walking far from their habitat. RedMark is a layered walk map for a Mars crew. It plans the fastest safe route to the next science target. Along the way, it works out where the crew is from photos instead of satellites. Our demo mission sends two astronauts, a robotic cart and a small drone into the Gale crater "boxwork" on Mount Sharp. The boxwork is a network of 1–2 m ridges with sandy hollows between them, and Curiosity has been studying it. The crew's job is to sample a ridge and a hollow that the rover never reached.

How it works

- Five map layers: base map and slope, walkability, science targets, conditions (radiation, weather, sun), and location quality.

- Route planning: finds the fastest safe route for the walkers and a separate route the cart can drive. When the system is less sure where the crew is, the route keeps further away from hazards.

- Position finding from photos, matched against NASA satellite maps and 3D terrain:

- Horizon fix: the skyline in a helmet-camera photo is compared with skylines calculated from 3D terrain. This gives the direction the astronaut is facing and a rough position.

- Ground fix: stereo photos of the nearby ground are matched to a 25 cm photo map for a precise position.

- Drone fix: a top-down drone photo is matched to the same photo map to place the astronauts.

- Every fix appears as a dot with an uncertainty circle and a confidence %. When confidence is low, the app asks for more photos.

Benefits and intended impact

RedMark gives crews a way to navigate that works offline, with no satellites, no compass and no live link to Earth. It also says how sure it is, because false confidence is dangerous. The location-quality layer shows where on the map position finding works well and where it doesn't, so planners can avoid places where the crew could get lost. Our goal is safer, more independent surface exploration, with samplelocations recorded precisely enough to be scientifically useful.

Tools and technologies

- Languages: Python 3.11 and TypeScript

- App: React, built with Vite

- Service: FastAPI

- Map and image processing: NumPy, rasterio, pyproj, Pillow, matplotlib

- Machine learning: PyTorch with the LoFTR image matcher, starting from weights JPL trained on HiRISE-scale maps

- Data:

- NASA/USGS HiRISE 3D terrain (1 m) and the photo mosaic (25 cm) of Gale

- MOLA global terrain for the distant skyline

- Curiosity Navcam photos and Ingenuity drone photos, used as stand-ins for astronaut and drone cameras

- Process: JSON Schema contracts between the four parts, GitHub with CI, and AI coding agents (Claude Code and Codex) working in parallel under human review

What makes it creative

Most Mars maps assume you already know where you are. RedMark makes position finding a core part of the map: it turns photos into a position and then measures how reliable that position is across the whole site. The route planner uses that measurement, so the path itself depends on how well the crew can be located.

Factors we considered

- Safety first: the fastest safe route, with hard limits and a rule that the crew can always walk back.

- Honesty: a 100% certain position is impossible, so every fix shows its uncertainty. Simulated results are always labelled as simulated.

- Map detail: the 1 m terrain barely shows the 1–2 m ridges, so we drew a ridge map from the 25 cm photos.

- Real-world limits: no astronaut photos exist, so we used rover and helicopter photos. Drone flights are short and fail over bland sand, so the helmet camera is always the main source. Messages to Earth take 4–24 minutes, so everything runs offline.

- Fair testing: we tested the matchers on a held-back set of rover photos that weren't used to tune them. The photos were split by stretch of the rover's route, so the same spot never appears in both sets.
